name: Connecticut

counties.09130: Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Region

notes: Food for home is exempt, but candy, gum and carbonated soft drinks are taxed at 6.35%, which is not counted here.
Alcohol bought at package stores pays 6.35% (7.35% when served), on top of per-gallon excise taxes left out here (spirits $5.94, still wine 79 cents, beer $7.20 a barrel).

Cigarettes and other tobacco pay 6.35%, on top of excise taxes left out here ($4.35 a pack of cigarettes; 40 cents a milliliter for closed e-cigarette systems and 10% of the wholesale price for open ones).
Household supplies: diapers are exempt since July 1, 2018, which is not taken out here.
Personal care products: feminine hygiene products are exempt since July 1, 2018, which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services: haircuts aren't taxed; nail and spa services (waxing, facials, body wraps) are, since July 1, 2011, which is not counted here.
Clothing is taxed (its under-$50 exemption ended July 1, 2011); items over $1,000 pay 7.75%. In the August 16 to 22, 2026 tax-free week, items under $300 were exempt.
Laundry and dry cleaning are taxed since January 1, 2020 (plus a 1% dry-cleaning surcharge, left out here); coin-operated self-service laundry, linen and uniform rental and tailoring aren't.

Gasoline is exempt from the sales tax and pays a 25-cent-a-gallon tax (since May 1, 2023) plus the 8.1% petroleum products gross earnings tax on its first sale in the state instead (about 51 cents a gallon in all, an estimate, not a DRS figure); there was no gas tax holiday in 2026; left out here.
Hotel stays pay a 15% state room occupancy tax (11% for bed and breakfasts); towns levy no hotel taxes; not counted here.

Vehicles over $50,000 and jewelry over $5,000 pay 7.75%; non-electronic school supplies are exempt from July 1, 2026; cannabis pays a single 10.75% state tax from October 1, 2026, plus an optional 3% town tax; none of these is counted here.
Towns levy no general sales tax; the only local tax on purchases is the optional 3% on cannabis.
gaps: No local sales taxes in Connecticut. Meals pay a higher state rate (7.35%), counted in the restaurant categories; towns may add 3% only on cannabis.

local: drawn from the city's parcels marked as in the zone (2023), with the streets between them

programs: Distressed municipalities are the Department of Economic and Community Development's 2025 list (37 towns, 12 of them in a grace period), mapped from the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection's layer. Hartford's Business Improvement District is mapped from the city's 2024 layer. New Haven's four special services districts, Stamford's Downtown Special Services District and towns' tax increment districts have no maps and are named on their pages; towns that aren't Census places can't be searched here (among them Bloomfield, with three tax increment districts, Windsor's Great Pond district and Cheshire's Interchange Zone, as reported by the law firm Pullman & Comley, not from a state list). The Department of Economic and Community Development lists 19 cities and towns approved for Enterprise Zones (Bridgeport, Bristol, East Hartford, Groton, Hamden, Hartford, Meriden, Middletown, New Britain, New Haven, New London, Norwalk, Norwich, Southington, Stamford, Thomaston, Waterbury, West Haven and Windham), where qualifying businesses can get a five-year, 80% local property-tax abatement. Bridgeport's zone is drawn from the city's map (its parcels in the zone, 2023); the other towns' zone boundaries (set by census tract) aren't published, so they aren't drawn. The Connecticut Main Street Center publishes no map.
Bridgeport's Steel Point tax increment district (as reported by the law firm Pullman & Comley, not from a state list) isn't mapped here.
Downtown Bristol's tax increment district (2018; as reported by the law firm Pullman & Comley, not from a state list) isn't mapped here.

warn.text: The Southeastern Connecticut planning region draws many visitors (Foxwoods, Mohegan Sun, Mystic and the shore), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the region as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Essex Village draws many visitors (the Connecticut River waterfront and the Essex Steam Train), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Mashantucket is home to Foxwoods Resort Casino, one of the largest in the country, but the census tract its page is built from isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. The site's lodging jobs come from Census business counts by county and ZIP code, which can miss or misplace a resort (a ZIP code with fewer than 3 lodging businesses has no row), so they likely read low here. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: New Haven's four special services districts (Town Green, Chapel West, Grand Avenue and Whalley Avenue) have no published map and aren't shown here.

Stamford's Downtown Special Services District has no published map layer and isn't shown here; Harbor Point's tax increment district (as reported by the law firm Pullman & Comley, not from a state list) isn't mapped either.
West Haven's development district (as reported by the law firm Pullman & Comley, not from a state list) isn't mapped here.

warn.text: Woodbury Center draws many visitors (its antique shops), but the census tract its page is built from isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Ledyard draws many visitors (Foxwoods Resort Casino, on the Mashantucket Pequot reservation in the town), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. The site's lodging jobs come from Census business counts by county and ZIP code, which can miss or misplace a resort (a ZIP code with fewer than 3 lodging businesses has no row), so they likely read low here. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
